1.pericope_label: Be not thou envious against evil men, neither desire to be with them ... through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established: and by knowledge shall the chambers be filled with all precious and pleasant riches
debates: Whom the studied destruction falls on: Gill takes it three ways, aimed at the good men who reprove them, at drawing others into their methods, and in the end at themselves; Henry and Keil and Delitzsch keep it on others, the latter grounding the warning in the risk of partnership.
Whether the filled chambers are literal or spiritual: Henry, Gill and Ellicott want both, Clarke keeps to the domestic sense.
outliers: Clarke supplies a chapter argument here rather than a note, laying out the topics to come in order.
Wesley makes the link between the two halves explicit, that there is no need to raise a family by ruining others when wisdom will do it more effectually.
themes: Envy answered by the prospect of honest gain
Piety and prudence both required
A house that will bear establishing

5.pericope_label: A wise man is strong ... for by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war ... wisdom is too high for a fool ... he that deviseth to do evil shall be called a mischievous person. The thought of foolishness is sin
debates: Whether the bare thought of evil is sin: Gill and Wesley take the inward motion itself to be forbidden by the commandment against coveting; Clarke denies that a simple thought about sin is sinful and locates the guilt in the purpose and the devising; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch support the second by the sense of the noun.

How the seventh verse should be rendered: Keil and Delitzsch report the usual sense, that wisdom is too high and costly for the fool, grant it is near the poet’s meaning, but object that it leaves the plural form unexplained and prefer an ornamental commodity above his station.
outliers: Clarke makes the wise man’s strength mechanical, since wisdom builds machines that do the work of a thousand men, and cites a Greek rendering preferring the wise to the strong.
Gill borrows the Stoic praise of the wise man, that he is happy, rich, mighty and a king, and claims it more truly for the good man.
themes: Wisdom as a kind of strength
The fool silent in the gate
Contrivance weighed against action

10.pericope_label: If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small. If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death ... if thou sayest, Behold, we knew it not; doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it?
debates: How the eleventh verse construes: Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading that makes the opening particle an oath, forbear not, I adjure thee, since the parallelism wants both classes of victim as objects of a single imperative, which all the old interpreters read as an imperative and none as an infinitive.

How wide the duty of rescue runs: Gill extends it to men taken by robbers, men unjustly sentenced and men drawn into snares of immorality or heresy; Henry extends it further, to travellers and ships in distress, and to those we owe no particular obligation.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch note the play on words between the strait and the strength, and quote a rendering that generalises it: he is not strong who is not firm in need.
Ellicott observes that the tenth verse leaves a man unable to help himself or others, and that a more excellent way follows in the eleventh.
Clarke holds that a man who through any pretence neglects to save an innocent life is guilty of blood.
themes: Courage measured by the day of trouble
A duty of rescue with no exemptions
An excuse that will not stand a second court

13.pericope_label: My son, eat thou honey, because it is good ... so shall the knowledge of wisdom be unto thy soul ... lay not wait, O wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous ... for a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again
debates: Whether the just man’s seven falls are into sin or into trouble: Ellicott, Wesley and Clarke read trouble and deny the other; Gill keeps both senses while preferring trouble as suiting the context; Henry works both and then decides for affliction rather than actual sin.

What the noun rendered a reward means: Clarke denies that it ever bears the sense of recompense, since its root refers to what is behind or last in time, and runs through seven versions to show that none understood it so, taking it of a future state; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch render it a future; Gill and Wesley keep the reward and its consolation.
outliers: Clarke insists from his own experience that the honeycomb is eaten, against the claim that it never is, and says no one who has not eaten it so can feel the force of the scriptural allusions.
Keil and Delitzsch note that the warning is aimed at the dwelling and resting-place rather than the person, and that two old translators misread a word and produced a sense without sense.
themes: Wisdom recommended by its sweetness
A future rather than a recompense
The righteous man who rises again

17.pericope_label: Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth ... lest the Lord see it, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him. Fret not thyself because of evil men ... for there shall be no reward to the evil man; the candle of the wicked shall be put out
debates: What the noun rendered reward means in the twentieth verse: Ellicott and Clarke read a future state, Clarke warning that the words hint at no annihilation since they concern the state of being and not being itself; Gill canvasses no good end, no hope of future things, and no posterity.
Where the turned wrath goes: Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all supply an upon thee, the punishment being lifted off the enemy and laid on the man who gloats.
outliers: Gill and Henry both allow a holy joy at the fall of the public enemies of God, and forbid only the joy of private revenge.

Clarke uses his note here to look back at the sixteenth verse and attack the reading that makes the seven falls seven daily sins, on the grounds that sin is not named, day is in neither the Hebrew nor any version, and the verb is never used of falling into sin.
themes: Gloating forbidden, holy joy allowed
A wrath that may change its object
Prosperity with no future in it

21.pericope_label: My son, fear thou the Lord and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change ... these things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment. He that saith unto the wicked, Thou art righteous
debates: What them that are given to change means: Henry presses the wording, that change for the better is not forbidden but change affected for its own sake; Clarke reads innovators always experimenting on forms of government and religion; Ellicott suggests those who think differently; Wesley, men unstable in their obedience.

Who wrote what follows the twenty-third verse: Clarke thinks a new section begins, perhaps from another collection; Ellicott makes the wise its authors; Gill reports the same rendering but thinks it more than probable the rest of the chapter is Solomon’s.
outliers: Henry holds that where the fear of God and of the king come into competition the case is adjudged, and we must obey God rather than men.
Keil and Delitzsch explain the two Hebrew idioms for partiality, lifting the face and regarding the face.
Gill limits the saying about calling the wicked righteous to a sentence pronounced in open court, not a private opinion.
themes: Religion and loyalty kept together
Change for its own sake
A judge who knows the truth and not faces

25.pericope_label: But to them that rebuke him shall be delight ... every man shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer. Prepare thy work without ... be not a witness against thy neighbour without cause ... say not, I will do so to him as he hath done to me
debates: How the kiss of the lips construes: Keil and Delitzsch reject the old versions, a passive reading the form will not bear, and a rendering that makes the lips the subject, and take the participle as subject; Ellicott reaches the same and glosses it that the words are as pleasant as a kiss.

What the twenty-seventh verse advises: Henry and Gill read household economics and the ordering of a great design, Keil and Delitzsch a warning against setting up a household before the conditions are met, Clarke doing nothing without a plan, Ellicott a method carried into the spiritual life.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch define the causeless witness as one with no substantial reason for testifying, not one ignorant of the facts, and remark in passing that the ancients, knowing nothing of the laws of sound, thought any derivation possible.
Henry warns that speaking only what is true is not enough if the manner of speaking insinuates otherwise, so that a man deceives by innuendo or hyperbole.
Ellicott calls the refusal of retaliation a wonderful anticipation of a later teaching; Keil and Delitzsch grant the talio a place in public justice but deny it validity on purely moral grounds.
themes: A rebuke that brings delight
Provision before building
Testimony and revenge both restrained

30.pericope_label: I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding; and, lo, it was all grown over with thorns ... yet a little sleep, a little slumber ... so shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth
debates: Whether the passage records a real observation or is framed as one: Gill thinks it very probably a matter of fact, Keil and Delitzsch describe it as a proverbial ode cast in the form of a record of experience.
outliers: Clarke devotes most of his note to the social standing of agriculture, the laws returning farms and remitting debts, and the absence in that commonwealth of suddenly raised fortunes, and contrasts his own country, where the merchant is all in all though property got at sea is as uncertain as the waves.
Clarke reads the last clause as an officer coming with an execution into the house, armed with the law, to take even the bed from under the slumberer.
Henry supports his lesson with an old saying that wise men profit more by fools than fools by wise men, since the wise avoid the faults of fools while fools will not imitate the virtues of the wise.
themes: A field left to the curse
Instruction taken from another man’s ruin
Poverty arriving on schedule
